title: Neural Bases of Subjective Control in Pain Processing
summary: The subjective feeling of helplessness can lead to increased pain perception. In chronic pain conditions helplessness is related to increased pain intensity reports. On the other hand, the feeling of subjective control over a painful experience decreased pain intensity reports in acute pain. An additional influence on pain perception are expectation effects as for example in placebo studies. The current study investigates if pain perception differs between a controllable and predictable (thus expected) painful stimulus, a predictable but uncontrollable painful stimulus and an uncontrollable and unpredictable painful stimulus in healthy subjects. Functional brain activity differences in pain and expectation processing brain areas are expected between the three different study conditions as well as activation differences of brain areas implicated in controllability estimation.

interventions.name:
Healthy participants that receive thermal pain stimuli in low, medium and high intensities during three experimental conditions (within-design): 
a) controllable and predictable pain 
b) uncontrollable and predictable pain 
c) uncontrollable and unpredictable pain

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
MRI-safety criteria
Exclusion criteria:
pregnant or nursing, acute or chronic pain, skin injury on arm, acute or chronic somatic or psychiatric illness (based on self-disclosure or professional examination), regular medication intake (except for allergy or thyroid medication, contraceptive medication, occasional use of pain medication), intake of painkillers in the 24 hours preceding the study appointment, symptoms of respiratory illness, contact with a Covid-19 case in the last 14 days
